newsitem.title: USA: Highlights of NYC comptroller report on '97 budget.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of NYC comptroller report on '97 budget.

text.p: Here are highlights of New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi's report on the Giuliani Administration's November modification to the 1997 fiscal budget, which the monitor released Tuesday.

The city's fiscal year ends June 30, 1997. --New York City could end the 1997 fiscal year with a surplus of more than $300 million if Wall Street's recovery, which has helped boost tax collection by $450 million more than first anticipated, continues.

--The city has as much as $543 million of resources that have not been recognized for fiscal year 1997, such as refundings by both the city and the Municipal Assistance Corp for New York City, as well as likely reductions in prior year payables and the General Fund.

--Saying it was too costly, Hevesi recommended that the city get out of a deal with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority that would have the agency give the city $250 million for operating expenditures in return for $500 million to finance mass transit improvements. He estimated the deal would cost taxpayers $1.2 billion over $25 years.

--The $200 million of risks remaining in the 1997 fiscal budget are balanced by the up to $543 million of resources, producing a potential budget surplus of $338 million to $343 million. The biggest risks remain the Board of Education, as it has uncertain claims for prior year state aid, and the overtime budget.
--The city cut the risk of overtime spending by adding $91 million to its overtime budget for this year and raising funding in future years.

--The rise in tax revenues primarily stems from higher business tax collections from Wall Street firms and might prove temporary. Further, there does not seem to be a "general strengthening in city's overall economy," Hevesi said.

--The city removed $588 million in questionable gap-closing measures from the 1997 fiscal budget but in some cases just moved them to next year. For example, Hevesi said the city is unlikely to get $270 million in back rent from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, though it moved the funds to the 1998 fiscal year.

--The city will spend about $25 million less than expected for training and travel expenses of Work Experience Employees who must work for the city to get public aid. Hevesi recommended the savings be used for training and day care requirements to meet the demands of new federal welfare law.

--There are $777 million of risks to the 1997 capital budget because the Wicks Law governing construction contracts has not been appealed, the state legislature has not approved a new infrastructure finance authority, and the city still expects to get $607 million by selling its water and sewer system, a move Hevesi has blocked in court. That battle is not expected to conclude until early next year.
--The November budget modification includes $1.23 billion in one-shots in fiscal year 1997, down from $1.5 billion in the budget that was adopted.
